# The authored spec corpus (`specs/`)
`specs/` used to hold only the grammar (`specs/schema/auger-spec-1.0.xsd`), so every XML document in the repository was a test fixture and nothing exercised the machinery `auger spec` ships. This directory is now the authored corpus: three documents about Auger's own XML-spec surface, written against the same grammar a consumer would use, with every test obligation naming a tracked test in this repository.
| Document | Document id | Blocks | Scope token | What it contracts | |---|---|---|---|---| | `specs/spec-graph.xml` | `AUGER-SPEC-GRAPH` | 3 | `auger.spec.load` | The corpus loader and the one-verdict rule shared by `spec validate` / `spec check`, including the XSD backstop. | | `specs/spec-verbs.xml` | `AUGER-SPEC-VERBS` | 4 | `auger.spec.select` | Block selection (`--id/--kind/--applies-to/--status/--version`), assembly closure, `--no-deps`, and the `empty-selector` refusal. | | `specs/verification.xml` | `AUGER-SPEC-OBLIGATIONS` | 5 | `auger.spec.obligation` | Where `path`/`selector` resolve (`--repo-root`, the consuming repository) and what `runner` means (a registry id, never a shell string). |
Twelve blocks in total: 4 requirements, 1 acceptance, 7 verifications. Block ids are stable and never renumbered; `kind` always equals the element name.

## Validating and reading it
Run from the repository root. The XSD processor (`lxml`) is a `dev` extra, not a runtime dependency, so a host without it refuses with `xsd-processor-missing` instead of passing.
```bash python auger.py spec validate specs # spec: 3 document(s), 12 block(s), 7 reference(s) ok
python auger.py spec check specs # {"nodes": ["SPEC-GRAPH-CORPUS", ...], "status": "valid"}
python auger.py spec list specs # one TSV line per block: id, kind, status, version, source, applies-to
python auger.py spec list specs --kind requirement python auger.py spec bundle specs SPEC-OBL-RUNNER # {"id":"SPEC-OBL-RUNNER","verifications":[{"path":"tests/test_verification_graph.py", ...}]}
python auger.py spec assemble specs --applies-to auger.spec.select --format json # matched blocks + closure, each carrying its source citation (spec-verbs.xml#SPEC-VERBS-SELECTION) ```
`spec validate` and `spec check` are one verdict from one loader: same exit code, same diagnostic. `spec assemble` never touches a test path, so it needs no `--repo-root`; `validate`, `check` and `bundle` do resolve obligations and use `--repo-root DIR` when the corpus lives outside the repository it describes. This corpus lives inside the repository it describes, so `git rev-parse --show-toplevel` from `specs/` is the root and no flag is needed.

## Querying the corpus as of a past version (AUG-167)
`spec list` and `spec assemble` accept `--as-of REF`: the corpus subtree is materialised as it existed at that git ref (the repository is resolved from the spec root, the subtree is extracted with `git archive` into a temp directory, and the ordinary selection path runs over it — read-only, no `.git` mutation, the temp dir is removed when the verb returns). `--as-of HEAD` is byte-identical to plain selection, and an earlier commit returns the block bodies as they were THEN. Four typed refusals, each `spec error (<code>)` on stderr with exit 2:
* `as-of-unknown-ref` — REF does not resolve in the repository; * `as-of-not-a-repository` — the spec root is not inside a git work tree; * `as-of-corpus-missing` — the corpus path does not exist at REF; * `as-of-git-unavailable` — the git executable is not available.
`--as-of` is a selection-verb flag only: `validate`, `check`, `bundle` and the other spec verbs refuse it. Superseded/successor chains are NOT rewritten across versions — a historical query returns the historical corpus exactly as the loader sees any corpus.

## The generated views
The XML is the source and the readable documents are views of it. Two views ship, rendered from the SAME loaded corpus: [`SPEC-CORPUS-VIEW.md`](SPEC-CORPUS-VIEW.md) and [`SPEC-CORPUS-VIEW.html`](SPEC-CORPUS-VIEW.html) — every document, every block with its prose and attributes, the measured counts, and a reference index of every typed edge. Both are committed, generated artifacts:
```bash auger spec render specs --out docs # rewrite both views (the CLI form, AUG-139) python3 scripts/gen_spec_view.py # the same renderer from a bare checkout python3 scripts/gen_spec_view.py --check # rc 1 when a committed view has drifted from specs/ ```
`auger spec render` reads the corpus through `auger.load_spec_corpus` — the loader every other `spec` verb uses — and writes `SPEC-CORPUS-VIEW.md` and `SPEC-CORPUS-VIEW.html` into `--out`, which must be an existing directory OUTSIDE the corpus root (`render-into-corpus`): a view written back into the source tree would be the second, editable copy this corpus exists to prevent.
`tests/test_spec_corpus_view.py` and `tests/test_spec_render.py` regenerate the views and assert BYTE equality with the committed files, so a view cannot drift from its source; the same tests prove the views are derived — an edit to ONE block's body moves that block's section in BOTH views and leaves every untouched block byte-identical. Edit the XML, then regenerate; a hand edit of either view fails those tests.

## The brief-context builder (AUG-165)
At dispatch time the factory foreman runs `python3 scripts/brief_spec_context.py --row <ROW-ID> --spec-root specs [--repo-root <git-top>]` and embeds what it prints into the worker brief. The builder resolves the row through the module's own API (`auger.build_spec_context` — the same selection `spec context` serves) and emits the selected blocks VERBATIM as a Markdown section, one heading per block carrying that block's own byte count and a header carrying the measured `input_bytes`.
The exit-code contract is the seam's whole point:
* **0 with a section** — the row is scoped by a `<task>` block; the blocks are embedded byte for byte. * **0 with NO section** — the row has no spec references (`unscoped`/`inactive`/zero selection): the brief gets **zero bytes, never an empty "SPEC CONTEXT" heading**, one honest line names the reason (`unknown-task`, …) on stderr, and `--status-json FILE` records the machine-readable outcome (`no-context`). * **3** — the answer is `ambiguous`: nothing is emitted and the candidate ids go to stderr so the tick report surfaces the ambiguity instead of a brief that guessed. * **2** — a typed auger refusal (missing spec root, unreadable corpus), with the auger error text unchanged on stderr.
A no-context answer is a normal outcome (the shipped corpus scopes no rows yet), not an error; an ambiguous answer is never silent.

## The spec-to-build loop, on a runnable example (AUG-206)
Eight more subverbs walk ONE task from a `<task>` block to a canonical board row and its judge packet — `task-packet`, `plan-draft`, `plan-approve`, `plan-export` (or the single-task `task-export`), `plan-reconcile`, `judge-packet`, `judge-handoff` — and every hand is bound to a digest (`sha256` of the canonical artifact), so nobody can approve a plan they are not looking at. `docs/VERBS.md` § spec documents each verb's flags and refusals; this section works the chain command by command on a corpus that ships in this repository.
**The runnable corpus: `docs/spec-example/tracker-loop.xml`.** It validates as-is in this checkout (the fenced block below is byte-identical to the whole file — declaration and copy-me comment included, verified by `scripts/check_spec_example.py`), and it is a template: copy the directory into your own repository and rename the ids. The verification block deliberately uses `method="inspection"` — a `method="test"` verification names a runner plus a git-tracked path/selector in the consuming repository (see § *Test obligations* in docs/XML-SPEC-SCHEMA.md), which a copied example would refuse until your own test exists — so the example resolves NO test obligation and validates anywhere.
```xml <?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?> <!-- A RUNNABLE spec-to-build example (AUG-206): one task, one plan, one approval surface.
This corpus validates as-is in this repository (`auger.py spec validate docs/spec-example`) and it is also a template: copy the directory into your own repository and rename the ids. The verification blocks deliberately use method="inspection" so the example resolves NO test obligation — a method="test" verification must name a runner plus a git-tracked path/selector in the repository that CONSUMES the corpus (docs/XML-SPEC-SCHEMA.md § Test obligations), and a copied example would refuse there. Turn the inspection into a real obligation once your own test exists and is tracked. --> <spec xmlns="urn:auger:spec:1" id="EXAMPLE-TRACKER-LOOP" version="1.0.0" schema-version="1.0">
<requirement id="EXAMPLE-REQ-1" kind="requirement" status="active" version="1.0.0" applies-to="auger.plan" verification="test" verifies="EXAMPLE-VER-1"> The exported plan produces one canonical board row per task, carrying the task's acceptance criteria verbatim and the plan digest the approval bound. </requirement>
<verification id="EXAMPLE-VER-1" kind="verification" status="active" version="1.0.0" applies-to="auger.plan" method="inspection"> Inspection here on purpose: a runnable example must not name a test file the consuming repository does not track. Replace this block with method="test" runner="pytest" path="tests/<your file>.py" selector="<your test>" once the real test exists. </verification>
<requirement id="EXAMPLE-REQ-9" kind="requirement" status="active" version="1.0.0" verification="inspection"> Batch export of several plans in one run, and the judge-handoff dispatch leg, are a later wave's work — the exclusion below keeps them visible and explained. </requirement>
<acceptance id="EXAMPLE-AC-1" kind="acceptance" status="active" version="1.0.0" applies-to="auger.plan" verification="test" verifies="EXAMPLE-REQ-1"> The canonical row's acceptance-criteria text equals this block's body exactly; a drifted row is repaired through `boardctl update`, never left behind. </acceptance>
<task id="EXAMPLE-TASK-1" kind="task" status="active" version="1.0.0" applies-to="auger.plan" verification="test" plan="EXAMPLE-PLAN" plan-version="1.0.0" in-scope="EXAMPLE-REQ-1" acceptance="EXAMPLE-AC-1" out-of-scope="EXAMPLE-REQ-9"> Export this plan's one task as one canonical board row, with the acceptance criteria embedded verbatim and the ch:trace marker binding row, spec blocks, test obligation and witness. <exclusion ref="EXAMPLE-REQ-9" reason="owned by the later wave; not this plan's reviewed scope"/> </task>
</spec> ```
The `<task>` element is the one block the loop orbits, and its attributes are exactly what the loop reads: `plan=` + `plan-version=` author plan membership (`plan-draft` refuses a plan whose members disagree on the version), `in-scope=` / `acceptance=` / `out-of-scope=` are the three id lists that become the packet's scope, and each child `<exclusion ref= reason=>` carries the reason an out-of-scope block is left out — out-of-scope without a reason refuses to validate. A `<task>` block is always plan-bound and approval-gated; a task packet is never built from a board row's prose.
**Driving the loop** (from the repository root; `auger.py` stands for the entry point):
```bash python auger.py spec validate docs/spec-example # spec: 1 document(s), 5 block(s), 5 reference(s) ok
# 1. the packet, and the digest an approval will be bound to python auger.py spec task-packet docs/spec-example --task EXAMPLE-TASK-1 # {"digest": "877d69ee...", "packet": {...}} — the packet digest an approval is bound to
# 2. the plan: many tasks, ONE version, ONE digest python auger.py spec plan-draft docs/spec-example --plan EXAMPLE-PLAN # {"plan": "EXAMPLE-PLAN", "version": "1.0.0", "digest": "07828ee7...", "tasks": [...]}
# 3. the approval — bound to that digest, naming WHO decided; the ledger (append-only, # default <spec root>/.auger/plan-approvals.jsonl) records the current UTC time unless # --at TIMESTAMP says otherwise python auger.py spec plan-approve docs/spec-example --plan EXAMPLE-PLAN --approve \ --digest 07828ee7e1b1bd9b50d4645db7e0d7501012efb23859e44ca009e4131114e632 --approver you # {"status": "recorded", "record": {"plan": "EXAMPLE-PLAN", "decision": "approved", "at": "2026-...", ...}}
# 4. the board rows — the FIRST board-writing step; the approval is checked before any # boardctl call, so the digest above gates every byte python auger.py spec plan-export docs/spec-example --plan EXAMPLE-PLAN --board <your board dir>
# 5. the judge leg — the packet GitReins' TaskPacketAdapter consumes, with the board's # acceptance criteria verbatim; hand it off with judge-handoff --dispatch-cmd <command> python auger.py spec judge-packet docs/spec-example --plan EXAMPLE-PLAN \ --row EXAMPLE-TASK-1 --board <your board dir> --boardctl boardctl
# 6. read the board's evidence back — read-only, writes: none python auger.py spec plan-reconcile docs/spec-example --plan EXAMPLE-PLAN --board <your board dir> ```
`--trace MARKER` on `judge-packet`/`judge-handoff` validates an ALTERNATIVE marker than the one bound into the approved row — a marker you would copy from the packet (`spec task-packet … | jq -r .trace`), never hand-write: the finding codes and marker rules are docs/XML-SPEC-SCHEMA.md § *The staged-diff checker*.
Fail-closed everywhere, in the same typed shape (`spec error (<code>)`, exit 2, nothing written): a digest that is not the plan's current one refuses `stale-plan-digest` ("approve the plan you are actually looking at"); exporting without an approval refuses `unapproved-plan-digest`; a `--task` id that is not a `<task>` block refuses `unknown-task` (naming that a task packet is built from a `<task>` block, never from a board row's prose); `spec plan-approve` against a 000…0 digest therefore never touches the ledger.

## What the corpus deliberately does not claim
* No block describes `init`, `start`, `ask`, `answer`, `check`, `status`, `toggle`, `dump` or `recall`. They are real verbs, but no requirement block here would be verified by a test obligation that this corpus can name honestly, so the corpus stays on the surface it can prove. * The generated view reports only what the loader reads. It does not judge the corpus: `spec validate` / `spec check` remain the verdict, and the view is a rendering of the same data.

## Authoring rules this corpus follows
1. Read `specs/schema/auger-spec-1.0.xsd` and `docs/XML-SPEC-SCHEMA.md` first. The grammar is loaded by a real XSD 1.0 processor on every verb, so an undeclared attribute is a refusal (`schema-invalid`), not a warning. 2. Every block needs `id`, `kind`, `status` and `version`; ids match `^[A-Z][A-Z0-9]*(-[A-Z0-9]+)+$` and are unique corpus-wide; `kind` equals the element name. 3. `requirement` and `acceptance` carry `verification=`; `verification` carries `method=`. `applies-to` is a whitespace-separated list of scope tokens. 4. A verification block that points at a test carries `runner="pytest"`, `path=` a repository-relative **tracked** file, and `selector=` a function that exists in that file. The validator resolves the path in the consuming repository, runs `git ls-files`, and parses the file's AST. 5. Reference direction has one owner per edge. A requirement names its test obligations with `verifies=` (that is what `spec bundle` reads); a verification block must not name that requirement back on the same edge pair — the loader refuses the resulting cycle with `reference-cycle`, which is why no verification block here carries `verifies=`.

## Product behaviour worth knowing when editing the corpus
* `spec check` reports only `requirement`, `verification` and `test` nodes, so the acceptance block (`SPEC-VERBS-SELECTION-AC1`) is validated by the grammar and by selection but never appears in the `check` node list. * Assembly closure follows forward `depends-on` plus inverse `verifies`. Selecting a requirement pulls the blocks that name it (its acceptance criteria); it does **not** pull the verification blocks the requirement's own `verifies=` names. Use `spec bundle <requirement>` for those.
